title: How to Tell Whether a Local Business Is Still Open Before You Contact It
dek: Learn which signals reliably show whether a local business is still operating, from listing hours to phone checks, before you spend time on outreach.

body_sections.heading: Why Open Status Is Harder to Confirm Than It Looks
paragraphs: Before you spend time on a call, an email, or a drive across town, it helps to know whether the business is operating at all. Closing a business is not a single synchronized event. A company can stop answering the phone weeks before the storefront goes dark. It can keep the lights on while it winds down, still paying rent on a lease that has not expired. It can also sell to a new owner who keeps the name but drops the services you were planning to discuss.

That lag creates the real problem for outreach: different sources go stale at different speeds. A directory listing might be two years out of date. A social account might be dormant but still online. A voicemail greeting might say "we're open Monday through Friday" months after the last employee left.

The practical approach is not to hunt for one definitive source. It is to gather several signals that update at different rates, compare them, and treat disagreement as useful information rather than noise. This article walks through the checks in the order that tends to resolve the question fastest.

body_sections.heading: Start With the Listings Owners Update Most Often
paragraphs: Business profiles on search engines and map apps are usually the first place owners edit when something changes, because those listings drive walk-in traffic and calls. That makes them a good early indicator, though not a final answer. For a detailed checklist of the profile fields that matter before outreach, see What to Check on a Google Business Profile Before You Reach Out.

body_sections.heading: Read the Status Label, Not Just the Star Rating
paragraphs: Most major map and search platforms let owners or visitors mark a business as permanently closed or temporarily closed. Look for that label near the business name. A "permanently closed" tag is a strong signal, but it is worth a second check, because competitors, former employees, and users can submit closure reports that owners may not notice or correct quickly.

body_sections.heading: Compare Hours Against the Current Date
paragraphs: Hours fields are frequently wrong in ways that look fine at a glance. A profile showing "Open now" may simply be running on a schedule nobody has updated since the owner changed staffing. Check whether the posted hours include recent holiday adjustments or notes such as "closed for renovation" or "appointments only." Seasonal businesses often show misleading status during their off months, so a single closed day proves very little.

body_sections.heading: Look for Recent Owner Activity
paragraphs: Photos uploaded by the owner, responses to reviews, and recent posts all indicate someone is actively managing the profile. A profile with no owner activity for a long stretch is not proof of closure, but it does suggest the business is not paying close attention to its online presence, which is a different problem worth noting before outreach.

body_sections.heading: Check the Website for Signs of Life
paragraphs: A website is heavier to maintain than a listing, so the signals there tend to be more meaningful, even if they update more slowly.

spans.text: A website is heavier to maintain than a listing, so the signals there tend to be more meaningful, even if they update more slowly.

body_sections.heading: Content Freshness
paragraphs: Look at the most recent blog post, news item, or event notice. Check the copyright year in the footer, though be careful: many sites never update that line even when the business is thriving, so treat it as weak evidence. Stronger signals include a current promotion with a date range, an updated menu or service list, or a staff page that reflects recent hires.

body_sections.heading: Contact Details That Match Elsewhere
paragraphs: Compare the phone number and address on the website against the map listing and any directory entries. When these drift apart, it often means the business moved, changed ownership, or stopped maintaining one of the two. A mismatch is a prompt to verify, not an automatic disqualifier.

body_sections.heading: Broken or Expired Elements
paragraphs: An expired security certificate, a contact form that returns an error, or a domain parked with an ad page are all signs that nobody is tending the site. Any one of these could have a technical explanation. Several together usually point to a business that has gone quiet.

body_sections.heading: Verify by Phone, but Listen for More Than a Ring
paragraphs: A call is still one of the most direct checks available, and it takes less than a minute. What matters is how you interpret the result.

Call during stated business hours rather than at random. If the business is appointment-based, try the booking link on the website or listing, since a live calendar with open future slots is a decent indicator that someone is still scheduling work. For a broader framework on reachability across lead sources, see How to Check for Contactability in Local Business Leads.
bullets: A person answers and can describe current services: strong evidence the business is operating.
A voicemail greeting with a recent-sounding update: moderately useful, but greetings can persist long after closure.
A generic carrier message or "the number you have dialed is not in service": a serious red flag.
Ringing with no answer at all, repeatedly, during posted business hours: ambiguous, and worth pairing with another check.

body_sections.heading: Look at Local and Social Signals
paragraphs: These checks are less authoritative on their own but useful for filling gaps.

body_sections.heading: Social Accounts
paragraphs: A business page with posts from the last few weeks suggests active operation. A page with nothing for a year tells you the account is dormant, which may or may not reflect the business itself. Some owners abandon social media entirely while remaining fully operational, so weigh this signal alongside the others.

body_sections.heading: Recent Reviews and Local Coverage
paragraphs: Reviews mentioning a recent visit carry more weight than older ones. Local news coverage, chamber of commerce mentions, or community event listings can confirm recent activity. Again, absence of recent coverage means little; plenty of healthy small businesses never appear in local media.

body_sections.heading: Cross-Check Registries, Licenses, and Filings
paragraphs: When you need a firmer answer, public records are worth the extra few minutes.

State business registries typically show whether an entity is active, dissolved, or delinquent on filings. Licensing boards for trades, health, and professional services often publish license status and expiration dates. A lapsed license does not always mean the business closed, but for regulated industries it is a meaningful signal.
These records also lag. A business may have closed months ago while its registration still shows active, because renewals are annual or biennial. Use registries to confirm life, not to prove death.

Phone disconnected or consistently unanswered during posted hours.
Website expired, parked, or frozen in a past year.
No reviews in a long stretch for a business that previously had regular ones.
License expired and registry status delinquent.
Recent owner replies to reviews or fresh photos on the listing.
A booking system with available future appointment slots.
A phone answered by someone who can discuss current services.
Current promotions, dated content, or event notices on the site.
Active license with a future expiration date.

body_sections.heading: What to Do When the Answer Is Unclear
paragraphs: Sometimes the checks produce a split verdict: the listing looks current, the phone goes unanswered, and the registry shows a delinquent filing. In that case, treat the business as unverified rather than closed.

A short, low-cost approach works well here. Try a different channel, such as email or a contact form, and see whether anything comes back. Look for a second location or a parent company if the business appears to be part of a group. Check whether the owner has another active business at the same address, which sometimes explains odd records.

Most importantly, do not record an unverified business as confirmed open in your outreach list. Mark the status clearly, note which signals you checked and when, and set a review date. Freshness is not a one-time determination. A business that looks active today can close next month, and a list built six months ago will contain stale entries no matter how careful the original research was.

body_sections.heading: Build This Into a Repeatable Pre-Outreach Step
paragraphs: The checks above take a few minutes per business and can be done in a consistent order: listing status, website freshness, phone, then records if the picture is still unclear. Doing them in the same sequence each time makes the results comparable and makes it obvious when a record needs rechecking.

It also keeps your outreach honest. Contacting a business that closed last year wastes your time and can look careless if the recipient is a former owner or a landlord. Verifying first is a small habit that pays off across an entire list.
If you want to go deeper on the research side before you start reaching out, a broader guide to researching a local business before sales outreach can help you decide what to collect and why.
